title: Universal Dynamic Scaling of 2D Quantum Ising Transition on the Fuzzy Sphere
authors: Meng Zeng, Shuai Yin, Roderich Moessner
abstract: We revisit the problem of \textit{real-time} quantum dynamics of the paradigmatic two dimensional transverse-field Ising model using the recently developed fuzzy sphere regularization scheme. By linearly ramping the transverse field from the paramagnetic phase to criticality, we study the finite-time scaling behavior of the squared order parameter $\langle m_z^2 \rangle$, the excitation energy density $Q$, and the two-point correlation function of $m_z$. We establish numerically that, at intermediate quench rate, $\langle m_z^2 \rangle$ follows the conventional Kibble-Zurek prediction set by the critical exponents of the $3$D Ising universality class, and the correlation function exhibits the expected exponential decay whose correlation length can be used to estimate the non-universal scaling coefficient in the freeze-out time/length. In contrast, the excitation energy density $Q$ does not reach the same scaling regime at available system sizes due to large effective finite-size gap from symmetry-enforced level sparsity in the energy spectrum. At slow quench rates the universal quasi-adiabatic scaling for both $\langle m_z^2 \rangle$ and $Q$ is recovered. Since the fuzzy sphere construction can realize not only the Ising conformal field theory (CFT), but a broad family of $(2+1)d$ CFTs, our results establish a route to the real-time critical dynamics of strongly coupled CFTs that are otherwise computationally challenging to study.
summary: This work analyzes the real-time evolution of the 2D transverse-field Ising model on a fuzzy sphere as it passes through a quantum critical point. By simulating observables like magnetization and correlation functions during controlled quenches, the authors confirm predictions from Kibble-Zurek theory for certain quantities. Crucially, they demonstrate that this method provides a powerful tool to study non-equilibrium dynamics in strongly coupled Conformal Field Theories.
main_problem: The study investigates the real-time quantum dynamics of a system driven through a continuous phase transition, specifically testing Kibble-Zurek scaling and finite-time scaling in two dimensions.
main_result: The squared order parameter $\langle m_z^2 angle$ successfully follows conventional Kibble-Zurek predictions at intermediate quench rates, while the fuzzy sphere construction provides a route to studying real-time dynamics of strongly coupled CFTs.
method: Numerical simulations using Time-Dependent Variational Principle (TDVP) on an effective Hamiltonian derived via fuzzy sphere regularization, supplemented by Exact Diagonalization for benchmarking.
model_or_system: The paradigmatic two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model realized on the fuzzy sphere geometry. The system is quenched by linearly ramping the transverse field across its critical point.
key_observables: Squared order parameter $\langle m_z^2 angle$, excitation energy density $Q$, and the two-point correlation function $C(	heta)$.
important_parameters: Quench rate ($v$), system size ($L$ or $N$), and the quench regimes (adiabatic, intermediate, fast).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on finite-size scaling arguments; a key limitation is that symmetry constraints cause the excitation energy density $Q$ to fail to reach predicted scaling regimes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate data collapse for $\langle m_z^2 angle$ and $C(	heta)$ confirming KZM, while also showing evidence of level sparsity in the energy spectrum due to symmetries.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model (Ising on fuzzy sphere), details the quench protocol, analyzes three key observables ($\langle m_z^2 angle$, $Q$, $C(	heta)$) across different quench rates, and concludes by generalizing the findings to other strongly coupled CFTs.
why_interesting: The combination of non-equilibrium dynamics (quenches), critical phenomena scaling laws (KZ theory), and advanced mathematical frameworks like fuzzy geometry makes this highly relevant for understanding universal behavior in many-body quantum systems.
